summary: Pages 47-113 and 134-137 of the host PDF are stray pages of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 22 (July 1947), misbound into the May 1948 issue; pages 114-133 are absent. The text is the tail of Section 1 (paragraphs 22-57) and fragments of Section 2 (Legal and Public Safety). Contents: Marshall's speech and Acting Military Governor Helmick's statements on American aid and food-export rumors; Korea Civil Service; the Interim Legislative Assembly's passage of the Anti-Collaborator Bill as the Special Law on National Traitors, Collaborators and Profiteers and its second reading of a Temporary Constitution; the dispute over transferring governors; Rightist and Leftist trends and the assassination of Lyuh Woon Hyung; verbatim American and Soviet statements on the Joint Commission deadlock over consultation with anti-trusteeship parties; mail exchanges, repatriation, courts, police installations and prison population. The identification as No. 22 / July 1947 is confirmed by the text: all dated events fall in July 1947 and the statistics refer to June 1947.
highlights: The Assembly completed second reading of the Anti-Collaborator Bill on 2 July, retitling it the Special Law Dealing with National Traitors, Collaborators, and Profiteers, with a three-year limit and no third reading.
Second reading of the Temporary Constitution passed all chapters by 31 July, dropping "democratic" from the title 31 to 8, and began local government (Section 36) on 31 July.
On 9 July the Assembly voted 39 to 22 to return the proposed transfer of four officials, ruling it lacked jurisdiction; on 28 July Kim Pyong No argued Ordinance 118 left Military Government supreme.
Leftist leader Lyuh Woon Hyung was shot dead in Seoul on 19 July by Hahn Chi Kun, and the Nation Saving Society was ordered dissolved.
The Joint Commission deadlocked over consulting Anti-Trusteeship Committee parties; party tables showed 71 Rightist parties (19.3 million claimed members) against 75 Leftist (32.3 million).

The Acting Military Governor reported 91 million dollars of civilian supply aid, May 1946 to March 1947, including 395,836 metric tons of grain, and on 19 July denounced food-export rumors as malicious lies.
Lt. Gen. Albert C. Wedemeyer was announced as President Truman's special envoy to Korea, shifting Rightist attention from the Joint Commission.
June 1947 prisons held 19,833 inmates, of whom 17,216 were sentenced; South Korea had 1,977 police installations as of 1 February 1947.

sections.title: Section 1 (continued): Government and Politics, paragraphs 22-57
sections.summary: July 1947 general section, paragraphs 22-57: Marshall's speech and aid figures, civil service ratings, the Anti-Collaborator Bill and Temporary Constitution, Lyuh Woon Hyung's assassination, the Joint Commission deadlock, and interzone mail.

sections.title: American aid to Korea and food-export rumors
sections.summary: Marshall's 1 July speech rejecting charges of American imperialism was released in Korean 8 July. On 9 July the Acting Military Governor reported 91 million dollars of aid, including 395,836 tons of grain; on 19 July he denounced food-export rumors.

sections.title: Korea Civil Service
sections.summary: The Training Division completed Performance Rating Reports, required for the first time of provincial and national employees, due in the first fifteen days of August from staff with six months' service. Clerical examinations continued.

sections.title: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly: Anti-Collaborator Bill
sections.summary: The Assembly passed the remaining collaborator and profiteer paragraphs and on 2 July retitled the measure the Special Law Dealing with National Traitors, Collaborators, and Profiteers, adopting a three-year limit and omitting a third reading.

sections.title: The Temporary Constitution of Democratic Korea (Chosun)
sections.summary: A compromise revised draft was presented 7 July and passed to second reading 11 July despite Leftist protests. "Democratic" was dropped from the title, 31 to 8; chapters were adopted and local government began 31 July.

sections.title: Assignment of officials
sections.summary: On 8 July the Assembly debated the proposed transfer of governors Park Keun Hon, Sunn Min Ho and Park Chong Man and Chung Il Hyung. On 9 July it voted 39 to 22 to return the communication for lack of jurisdiction.

sections.title: Clarification of Assembly authority (Ordinance 118)
sections.summary: On 28 July Justice Director Kim Pyong No held that Ordinance 118 leaves Military Government supreme and able to legislate without Assembly approval; Suh U Sok and Yang Che Pak disputed this and cited the Assembly's power to review appointments.

sections.title: The Franchise Law
sections.summary: On 31 July the Assembly took up the Acting Military Governor's 21 July letter on franchise provisions, including the age limit of twenty-three. Members defended it; the matter went to the Legislative and Judicial Committee, 44 to 0.

sections.title: Attendance of representatives, July 1947
sections.summary: Table of Assembly sessions 102 to 120 in July 1947, with members present (55 on 15 July to 76 on 9 July, of 90 authorized) and presiding official. Quorum is 45 to hold session and 60 for measures.

sections.title: Political Activities: the Right
sections.summary: Rightist hopes for the Joint Commission fell in July. On 4 July, 150 representatives of about seventy organizations rejected General Brown's criticism and Hodge's letter to Rhee, demanded a general election and Ahn's resignation.

sections.title: Political Activities: the Left
sections.summary: The Left sought to exclude Rightists from consultation; nine parties issued statements on 10 and 19 July. Lyuh Woon Hyung was shot dead 19 July by Hahn Chi Kun, and the Nation Saving Society was ordered dissolved.

sections.title: Political Activities: General (Presidential envoy)
sections.summary: Announcement that Lt. Gen. Albert C. Wedemeyer would go to Korea as President Truman's special envoy brightened Rightist outlook and shifted attention from the Joint Commission; the Leftist press barely mentioned it.

sections.title: US-USSR Joint Commission
sections.summary: The Joint Commission met in Pyongyang 2-3 July, then deadlocked in Seoul over consultation with Anti-Trusteeship Committee parties. Brown (15 July) and Shtikov (21 July) stated positions; party tables list 71 Rightist and 75 Leftist parties.

sections.title: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Mail went north twice in July: 10,643 letters, 1,703 cards and 537 registered items on 12 July, and 10,108, 1,568 and 542 on 26 July. Smaller volumes came south each time.

sections.title: Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: As of 26 July, 18,672 Koreans entering Japan illegally were apprehended in Japan and 416 in Korean waters; 300 permits went to Chinese for repatriation. Dr. Moon Chang Wook left 22 July to find sponsors for fifty students.

sections.title: Section 2 (fragment): Legal and Public Safety
sections.summary: Fragment of Section 2 on legal and public safety: court docket and juvenile court figures, then police installations and the June 1947 prison population. Pages 114-133 are absent.

sections.title: Legal
sections.summary: Chief Justice Kim Young Moo's directive brought criminal dockets current by 20 July. Juvenile courts tried 1,240 cases in five months of 1947; twenty-nine probationers became judges and prosecutors; 2,500 law books went to the National Law Library.

sections.title: Public Safety: police installations and prisons
sections.summary: South Korea had 1,977 police installations on 1 Feb. 1947: 156 stations, 414 boxes, 1,495 sub-stations, 68 branches. Kwangju Prison used about 500 working prisoners; June 1947 prisons held 19,833, of whom 17,216 were sentenced.
